facts.statement: The species of this extinct bird is Sylviornis neocaledoniae.
facts.quote: species: neocaledoniae

facts.statement: The genus Sylviornis was named by Poplin in 1980.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Poplin, 1980

facts.statement: Fossils of Sylviornis date to the Holocene epoch.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Holocene

facts.statement: Sylviornis was a large, flightless bird endemic to New Caledonia in the Western Pacific.
facts.quote: Sylviornis is an extinct genus of large, flightless bird that was endemic to the islands of New Caledonia in the Western Pacific.

facts.statement: Sylviornis belongs to the extinct family Sylviornithidae and is related to the Galliformes group.
facts.quote: It is considered to constitute one of two genera in the extinct family Sylviornithidae, alongside Megavitiornis from Fiji, which are related to the Galliformes

facts.statement: Thousands of subfossil bones of Sylviornis have been found on New Caledonia and the nearby Île des Pins.
facts.quote: It is known from many thousands of subfossil bones found in deposits, some of them from the Holocene, on New Caledonia and the adjacent Île des Pins.

facts.statement: Sylviornis likely went extinct shortly after humans arrived in New Caledonia around 1500 BC.
facts.quote: It was likely hunted to extinction, shortly after the first human arrival to New Caledonia around 1500 BC.

facts.statement: Sylviornis stood about 80 cm tall and weighed between 27 and 34 kg.
facts.quote: Sylviornis was a huge flightless bird, around 80 cm tall, and weighing around 27-34 kg.

facts.statement: Sylviornis is the most massive pangalliform bird known to science.
facts.quote: It is the most massive pangalliform known to have ever existed.

facts.statement: Sylviornis had a large skull with a high, laterally compressed beak topped by a bony knob.
facts.quote: It had a large skull with a high and laterally compressed beak surmounted by a bony knob.

facts.statement: Sylviornis possessed unique skeletal features, including unfused clavicles, a high number of tail vertebrae, and a ribcage and pelvis resembling dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The skeleton has a number of peculiarities and differences that make Sylviornis stand apart from all other known birds: the clavicles were not fused to a furcula, the number of caudal vertebrae was very high, and the ribcage and pelvis were almost dinosaurian in appearance.

facts.statement: The wings of Sylviornis were reduced to small stubs.
facts.quote: The wings were reduced to small stubs.

facts.statement: Native accounts describe Sylviornis as reddish with a star-shaped head marking, capable of running fast using its wings for balance.
facts.quote: Native accounts believed to be based on Sylviornis describe a bird reddish in color, with a star-shaped calque on its head, and fast despite being flightless because it used its reduced wings for balance while running.

facts.statement: Sylviornis likely had a well-developed sense of smell and was active during twilight hours.
facts.quote: The anatomy of its skull suggests that it had a reduced optic lobes, with a well developed sense of smell and somatosensorial system, adapted for being active during twilight conditions (crepuscular) in search of food.

facts.statement: There is a debate over whether Sylviornis was a herbivore feeding on roots or a specialized invertebrate predator.
facts.quote: Because of its beak morphology and chicken-like feet, some authors guessed that the species was a herbivore that fed on low vegetation and dug up roots and tubers, but others that it was a specialized invertebrate predator.

facts.statement: Up to 50% of Sylviornis fossils found in some deposits belong to juvenile animals.
facts.quote: A large proportion—up to 50% in some deposits—of the remains found were from juvenile animals.

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that Sylviornis did not incubate its eggs but instead built large mounds similar to megapodes.
facts.quote: It was thought that the bird did not incubate its eggs but built a mound similar to the megapodes.

facts.statement: Large tumuli on Île des Pins, initially thought to be graves, are hypothesized to be incubation mounds built by Sylviornis.
facts.quote: Tumuli on the Île des Pins which were initially believed to be graves were found to contain no human remains or grave goods, and it has been hypothesized that they were the incubation mounds of Sylviornis.

facts.statement: Recent assessments suggest it is unlikely that Sylviornis was a mound-builder because it is not closely related to megapodes.
facts.quote: However, recent assessment of this bird as outside and not even particularly closely related to megapodes make the possibility that it was a mound-builder like them strictly unlikely.

facts.statement: Native accounts state that Sylviornis laid a single egg between November and April without incubating or protecting it.
facts.quote: In native accounts, the bird only laid one egg between November and April that was not incubated, covered, or protected in any way.

facts.statement: Adult Sylviornis were described as aggressive.
facts.quote: However, the adults were aggressive.

facts.statement: The most recent fossil evidence of Sylviornis is a bone from the Pindai Caves dated to 1120–840 BCE.
facts.quote: The most recent evidence of the species is a bone from the Pindai Caves carbon dated to 1120–840 BCE.

facts.statement: If native accounts are accurate, Sylviornis eggs and hatchlings would have been vulnerable to introduced mammalian predators.
facts.quote: If native accounts about its breeding habits are accurate, the eggs and hatchlings would also be vulnerable to introduced mammalian predators.

facts.statement: The parent group of the genus Sylviornis is the family Sylviornithidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Sylviornithidae

facts.statement: The time range for Sylviornis is the Holocene, from 0.0117 to 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Holocene to Holocene (0.0117 to 0 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Researchers theorize that Sylviornis laid clutches of 2 to 10 eggs and had an average lifespan of only 5 to 7 years.
rejected.quote: Thus, it has been theorized that Sylviornis had a clutch of at least two, more probably closer to 10 eggs, and that the average lifespan was not much more than 5–7 years

rejected.statement: Sylviornis is classified in the class Aves.
